result:
There’s a strange kind of magic hiding in the in-between places. Not the destinations—the airports, the lobbies, the hour after everyone has left the party and before the cleaning crew arrives. These are the liminal zones, the brief pauses where the world seems to hold its breath.

We spend so much energy rushing *through* them. We check our phones in empty hallways. We scroll through news in waiting rooms. We treat transitions like errors in the schedule, something to endure until real life resumes. But maybe that’s backward. Maybe the transition *is* the real part.

Think of the moment right after rain, when the pavement is still dark but the air smells like it’s been rinsed clean. Or the quiet in a house at 3 a.m., when even the refrigerator sounds like a distant ocean. These aren’t empty spaces; they’re full of a different frequency—slower, more honest. Without the pressure of performance, you can hear your own thoughts arranging themselves into shapes you didn’t know they had.

I like to believe that every day contains hidden doors like these, if you stop long enough to notice the hinge. The walk between your car and the front door. The silence after hanging up the phone. The first sip of coffee before the day claims you. They don’t ask for ceremony. They just ask for presence.

So here’s a small rebellion: don’t fill every gap. Let a few stay open. Let yourself exist in the draft, unfinished, for a minute or two. The world will keep spinning, but you might find that you’ve remembered how to listen to it.
